title: Introduction to Strongly Connected Components
description: Find groups of nodes in a directed graph that can all reach each other

sections.title: 1. What is a Strongly Connected Component?
12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: A strongly connected component, or SCC, is a group of nodes in a directed graph where every node can reach every other node in the group. It is the directed graph answer to the question which nodes are mutually reachable.
Finding SCCs breaks a tangled directed graph into clean, cycle free layers. Two elegant linear time algorithms exist for it: Kosaraju and Tarjan.

blocks.caption: A directed graph split into strongly connected components
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761243-271874592.png

By the end of this topic you will understand what an SCC is, why they matter, both classic algorithms and their code, the condensation graph they produce, the complexity, and where SCCs are used. It is a key tool for directed graphs.
SCCs turn the scariest looking directed graph into something orderly. Once you group the mutually reachable nodes, whatever remains between the groups can never form a cycle.
Both algorithms we cover run in linear time, so finding SCCs is cheap enough to use as a routine preprocessing step.

content.title: 1. What is a Strongly Connected Component?

blocks.text: In a directed graph, edges have a direction, so being able to go from u to v does not mean you can get back. A strongly connected component is a maximal set of nodes where you can travel from any node to any other and back again.

blocks.caption: Two nodes are in the same SCC when each can reach the other
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761243-718136082.png
blocks.alt: What is a Strongly Connected Component?

blocks.text: The word maximal matters: an SCC includes every node that is mutually reachable with the others, not just a subset. Every node belongs to exactly one SCC, even if that component is just the node by itself.

items: Defined only for directed graphs
Every pair of nodes in an SCC can reach each other
Each SCC is maximal, containing all mutually reachable nodes
Every node lies in exactly one SCC

blocks.text:
Mutual reachability:

The heart of an SCC is a two way trip. If you can get from u to v and also from v back to u, they belong together.
In the example graph, A, B, and C form one component because the edges A to B, B to C, and C to A let you loop among them freely.
Meanwhile D and E form a second component through their mutual edges, and the link from C to D joins the two components in one direction only.
SCCs let you understand the large scale structure of a directed graph by grouping together everything that is cyclically entangled.
Once you collapse each SCC into a single node, the messy directed graph becomes a clean acyclic one, which is far easier to reason about and to run further algorithms on.

items: They reveal cycles and feedback loops in directed graphs
They simplify a graph into cycle free super nodes
They expose which parts of a system are mutually dependent
They are a prerequisite for several higher level algorithms
They expose feedback loops and circular dependencies
They compress a graph into cycle free super nodes
They tell you which parts of a system are inseparable
They prepare a graph for topological reasoning

blocks.text: This is why SCCs are often the first step in analysing a directed graph: they replace a cyclic tangle with an acyclic skeleton you can walk in order.
Picture a directed graph as a network of one way streets. Two intersections are in the same SCC if you can legally drive from either one to the other and back.
A single directed cycle is the simplest SCC: every node on the cycle can reach every other by following the loop. Larger SCCs are just overlapping cycles woven together.

items: A directed cycle is the simplest strongly connected group
Overlapping cycles merge into a larger SCC
A node with no way back from its neighbours is its own SCC
SCCs partition the whole graph into such groups

blocks.text: The one way street analogy is worth holding onto: an SCC is a neighbourhood where you can always drive back to where you started, no matter which turns you take.

Direction is everything:

In an undirected graph, reachable and mutually reachable are the same. In a directed graph they differ, and that gap is exactly what SCCs measure.

items: A directed cycle is the simplest SCC
Overlapping cycles fuse into a bigger SCC
A lone node with no return path is its own SCC
Together the SCCs partition every node exactly once

blocks.text: Kosaraju algorithm finds all SCCs with two depth first passes and one graph reversal. It is remarkably simple to state.

blocks.caption: Kosaraju: DFS for finish order, reverse the edges, then DFS again
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761243-514954024.png

items: First, run a DFS over the graph and record the order in which nodes finish
Second, reverse the direction of every edge to get the transpose graph
Third, run DFS on the transpose, taking nodes in reverse finish order
Each DFS tree in that third pass is exactly one SCC

blocks.text: The magic is that processing nodes in reverse finish order on the reversed graph isolates each SCC perfectly, so no component leaks into another.
The beauty of Kosaraju is that each step is just an ordinary DFS you already know, plus a simple edge reversal in between.
Nothing about it requires clever bookkeeping during the search, which is why it is often the first SCC algorithm people learn.
Let us unpack why the three steps work. The first DFS orders nodes so that the last to finish sits in a source SCC, one that can reach others but is not reached back.

Reversing the edges flips that relationship. Now the source SCC becomes a sink in the transpose, so a DFS started there cannot escape its own component. Processing in reverse finish order peels off one SCC at a time.

Why the reversal works:

On the transpose graph, a DFS launched from the right node is trapped inside its SCC, because the only edges that would let it escape now point the other way.
Think of the finish order as ranking nodes by how late they wrap up. The latest finisher is guaranteed to sit in a component that can reach the others.
Reversing the edges then makes that same component a dead end, so a fresh DFS from it stays neatly contained.
If tracing this by hand feels abstract, just trust the recipe: finish order first, reverse the edges, then peel components in reverse finish order.
The implementation is two DFS routines and a reversed adjacency list.
Note the two visited arrays, one per pass, and the comp array that labels each node with its component number as the second DFS discovers it.
The count c at the end is both the number of SCCs and the labels zero through c minus one assigned to the nodes.
Tarjan algorithm finds every SCC in a single DFS, with no graph reversal, which makes it a favourite in practice.

blocks.caption: Tarjan uses one DFS with discovery indices and low links to root each SCC
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761243-867143263.png

As it explores, it gives each node a discovery index and tracks a low link, the smallest index reachable from that node. Nodes are pushed on a stack, and when a node low link equals its own index, everything above it on the stack forms one SCC.

items: Runs a single DFS, no reversal needed
Assigns each node a discovery index in visit order
Tracks the lowest index reachable, the low link
When low link equals the index, pop an SCC off the stack

blocks.text:
One pass elegance:

Tarjan folds all the work into one DFS. The low link value quietly detects when the search has finished exploring a whole strongly connected group.
Tarjan low link is the smallest discovery index reachable from a node, including through back edges to nodes still on the stack.
When a node cannot reach anything older than itself, it is the entry point of its component, and the stack above it is popped as one SCC.

items: Assign discovery indices in DFS visit order
Keep nodes on a stack as they are explored
Update low link from children and back edges
Pop an SCC when low link equals the discovery index

blocks.text: Both algorithms find all SCCs in linear time, so the choice is about style and constants.

items: Kosaraju: two DFS passes plus building the reversed graph, but very easy to understand
Tarjan: a single DFS with low links, no reversal, and often faster in practice
Kosaraju needs the transpose graph in memory; Tarjan does not
Both are O(V plus E) and both are widely used

blocks.text: Learn Kosaraju first for its clarity, then Tarjan when you want the single pass efficiency and do not want to build a reversed graph.
If you value clarity and do not mind two passes, choose Kosaraju. If you want a single pass and no reversed graph, choose Tarjan.
Because both are linear, this decision never affects the asymptotic running time, only constants and code style.

Once you have the SCCs, a powerful move is to build the condensation graph: collapse each SCC into a single super node, and draw an edge between super nodes wherever an edge crossed between their components.

blocks.caption: Collapsing each SCC into a super node yields a directed acyclic graph
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406761803-695968619.png

The result is always a directed acyclic graph, a DAG, because all the cycles were hidden inside the SCCs. That means you can topologically sort the condensation and reason about the graph in clean dependency order.

items: Each SCC becomes one super node
Edges between different SCCs become edges between super nodes
The condensation is guaranteed to be a DAG
You can topologically sort it to get a dependency order

blocks.text: The condensation is where SCCs pay off for other algorithms. Problems that need an acyclic graph can first collapse cycles away with this step.
For instance, longest path is hard on a general directed graph but easy on the acyclic condensation.
Both algorithms are optimal, touching every node and edge a constant number of times.

items: Time: O(V plus E) for both Kosaraju and Tarjan
Kosaraju does two traversals plus building the transpose
Tarjan does a single traversal with a stack
Space: O(V plus E) for the graph, plus O(V) bookkeeping

blocks.text: Linear time is the best possible, since you must at least look at every edge once to know the structure.
The linear bound assumes an adjacency list. With an adjacency matrix the traversal would cost O(V squared) simply to scan the edges.
In practice both algorithms are fast enough to run on graphs with millions of edges, which is why they appear inside larger pipelines so often.
SCCs show up whenever cycles and mutual dependency matter in a directed setting.

items: Detecting cyclic dependencies among modules or tasks
Solving 2 satisfiability by SCCs on an implication graph
Analysing the link structure of web pages and social networks
Simplifying a directed graph before running other algorithms

blocks.text: The 2 satisfiability use is especially neat: a formula is satisfiable exactly when no variable and its negation land in the same SCC of the implication graph.

items: Cyclic dependency detection in build systems and packages
2 satisfiability via an implication graph
Web and social network structure analysis
Compiler and dataflow analysis

blocks.text: The 2 satisfiability trick is a highlight: build an implication graph, find its SCCs, and the formula is solvable exactly when no variable shares an SCC with its own negation.

content.title: 12. Pitfalls and How to Approach It

blocks.text: Keep these points in mind when working with SCCs.

items: SCCs are a directed graph concept; on undirected graphs use connected components instead
A single node with no return path is its own SCC, which is easy to forget
For Kosaraju, be careful to process nodes in reverse finish order
Deep graphs can overflow recursion, so consider an iterative DFS or raise the limit

blocks.text:
How to spot an SCC problem:

Look for directed graphs where mutual reachability or cycles matter, or where you want to collapse cycles into a clean DAG. That is the SCC signal.
A common confusion is mixing up SCCs with weakly connected components, which ignore direction. SCCs strictly respect edge direction.
Strongly connected components reveal the cyclic backbone of a directed graph.

items: An SCC is a maximal group of mutually reachable nodes in a directed graph
Kosaraju uses two DFS passes and a graph reversal
Tarjan uses a single DFS with discovery indices and low links
Both run in linear O(V plus E) time
Collapsing SCCs yields a DAG you can topologically sort

blocks.text: Whenever a directed graph is tangled with cycles, find its SCCs to collapse the mess into a clean, acyclic structure you can actually reason about.
Carry this picture: one way streets grouped into neighbourhoods you can always loop around, with the neighbourhoods themselves forming a clean, cycle free map.
